strengths: Significance: RSD offers a useful efficiency–quality tradeoff for one-step super-resolution. Table 4 reports 174M parameters and 539 MB peak inference memory, compared with OSEDiff’s 1775M parameters and 3651 MB, while achieving competitive results on several benchmarks.

Empirical soundness: Improvements over the same-family ResShift and SinSR baselines are substantial and reasonably broad. On full-size RealSR, RSD improves LPIPS from ResShift’s 0.360 to 0.273 and MUSIQ from 59.873 to 65.860. Evaluations cover synthetic and real degradations, full images and crops, and an additional teacher trained on higher-resolution LSDIR images.

Methodology: The conditional-expectation argument underlying Proposition 3.1 provides a meaningful surrogate identity under an ideal, optimally fitted fake denoiser. Tables 5 and 6 help explain the contributions of timestep training and supervised losses.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript provides extensive comparisons, training pseudocode, optimizer settings, loss coefficients, baseline checkpoints, and dataset sources. Appendix H includes concrete failure cases and acknowledges hallucinated details, appropriately qualifying the practical results.
weaknesses: Soundness—central theoretical claim: The claimed equivalence between Eq. (7) and the trajectory KL in Eq. (9) is not established. Appendix A.1, page 19, replaces the reverse-chain marginal p(xt|y0) with q(xt|x̂0,y0), asserting equality. A conditional forward kernel is not its marginal mixture, and even the mixture over generator outputs need not equal the marginal of the finite-step Gaussian reverse chain defined in Eqs. (14)–(15). Consequently, the advertised distinction that RSD matches temporal dependencies through a joint trajectory KL is unsupported. The degenerate final transition and the practical omission of the derived timestep weights also require qualification.

Soundness—optimization claims: Proposition 3.1 relies on the fake model realizing the exact conditional expectation; finite neural-network training does not guarantee this. Ignoring the dependence of the optimal fake model on generator parameters requires an envelope-theorem argument and appropriate assumptions. The implementation instead uses five alternating fake-model updates and additionally trains its shared features adversarially. No analysis establishes how these approximations affect the claimed objective. Appendices A.2–A.3 also incorrectly change a negative minimum into a minimum of the negated expression; the latter should be a maximum.

Experimental attribution: The ResShift-VSD comparison does not isolate the proposed loss. Algorithm 2 trains its generator only at T, whereas RSD uses multistep training and additional noise conditioning. Table 5 shows that multistep training alone materially changes performance. A matched VSD baseline with identical timestep conditioning, architecture, supervised losses, and tuning is needed. Likewise, Table 6 never removes the RSD loss while retaining LPIPS and GAN losses, leaving its incremental benefit in the final system unresolved.

Originality: Appendix A.2 identifies the objective’s close correspondence to SiD at α=0.5 and FGM, and Appendix A.3 describes it as a discrete IBMD variant. These connections do not eliminate the value of adapting distillation to ResShift, but they narrow the novelty to an application and training configuration. The manuscript’s stronger theoretical novelty claims depend on the unsupported trajectory-KL interpretation, and experiments do not isolate the benefit of retaining the complete objective relative to these related formulations.

Evidence and scope: Better perceptual quality and fidelity than T2I methods are not consistent across datasets. On DRealSR crops, OSEDiff outperforms RSD in PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, MUSIQ, and MANIQA (Table 3). Selected visual examples and aggregate image-quality metrics do not establish systematically reduced hallucination; no human evaluation or targeted faithfulness assessment is provided. Results also lack uncertainty estimates across training or sampling seeds. Efficiency measurements use only 64×64 LR inputs on an A100, limiting conclusions about consumer-device or high-resolution deployment.

Reproducibility and presentation: Algorithm 1 samples generator timesteps uniformly from all T steps, conflicting with the selected N=4 configuration, and assigns added noise channels to the fake model while Appendix C describes adding them to the generator. Eq. (10) does not clearly specify the distinct discriminator and generator objectives. The exact loss normalization and an RSD implementation are not supplied in the manuscript. These ambiguities affect faithful reproduction.

Research ethics: The failure-case discussion is constructive, but Appendix H’s inference that standard, safe training images imply low misuse risk is unsupported. Its proposed medical and autonomous-driving applications should also acknowledge the consequences of plausible but incorrect reconstructed details.

strengths: Significance: RSD offers a useful practical improvement over existing ResShift distillation. On RealSR, Table 1 reports LPIPS improving from SinSR’s 0.365 to 0.273 and MUSIQ from 61.582 to 65.860, while maintaining single-step inference. Table 4 documents substantially lower parameter count and memory consumption than OSEDiff.

Empirical coverage is substantial: evaluation includes five datasets, synthetic and real degradations, full-image and crop protocols, multiple fidelity and perceptual metrics, and additional baselines in the appendices. Appendix E also investigates training at higher resolution.

Soundness: The conditional-expectation argument underlying Proposition 3.1 provides a reasonable idealized foundation for the auxiliary-model objective when the fake model attains the population regression optimum. Distillation-only results and timestep/loss ablations provide useful evidence beyond the final combined model.

Presentation and reproducibility: The overall method is understandable, and the manuscript supplies pseudocode, training hyperparameters, compute information, dataset sources, and baseline checkpoints. Appendix H candidly illustrates failures, including hallucinated details and poor reconstruction of complex textures.
weaknesses: Soundness—central theoretical claim: The asserted equivalence between Eq. (7) and the trajectory KL in Eq. (9) is not established. Appendix A.1 replaces a reverse-process marginal p(xt|y0) with q(xt|x̂0,y0), explicitly claiming they are equal. The latter is conditional on a particular generated image; integrating over generated images gives a forward-noised marginal, which is still not generally the marginal of the finite-step Gaussian reverse model defined in Eqs. (14–15). The derivation also includes t=1 despite its zero posterior variance and singular weight involving η0. Consequently, the central explanation that RSD improves on VSD through exact joint-trajectory matching is unsupported.

Soundness and presentation: Appendices A.2–A.3 incorrectly turn the negative minimum in Eq. (8) into a minimum of the negated objective; this should be a maximum. As written, the negative quadratic makes these minimizations unbounded below. Moreover, Proposition 3.1 assumes an optimal conditional-mean estimator, whereas training uses finitely many fake-model updates and additionally modifies its encoder through the GAN objective. The manuscript needs to distinguish its exact population identity from the implemented approximation.

Experimental attribution: The comparison against ResShift-VSD does not isolate the distillation objective. Algorithm 2 trains VSD only from the terminal timestep, whereas RSD uses multistep training, whose substantial effect is demonstrated in Table 5. The final RSD additionally uses LPIPS and GAN supervision. A matched comparison using the same timestep training, conditioning, supervision, and tuning budget is needed. Table 6 also lacks a supervised-only baseline, leaving the incremental benefit of distillation in the final system unclear.

Originality: Appendix A acknowledges close equivalence to SiD/FGM objectives and interprets RSD as a discrete IBMD variant; IBMD already includes image restoration. Adapting these ideas to latent ResShift and realistic degradations can be useful, but the claim of a novel objective is stronger than the demonstrated distinction. Direct controlled comparisons with these closely related formulations are missing.

Significance and claim calibration: Better fidelity than OSEDiff is not consistent across datasets. On DRealSR crops in Table 3, RSD has worse PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, MUSIQ, and MANIQA. Reduced hallucination is supported mainly by selected examples and aggregate image metrics, without a systematic content-faithfulness assessment. The efficiency advantage is strongest for memory and parameters; Table 4’s latency improvement over OSEDiff is relatively modest, 0.075 to 0.059 seconds, and measured only at 256×256 output resolution.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: Algorithm 1 samples all training timesteps despite the selected four-timestep configuration, and it adds noise channels to the fake model whereas Appendix C describes adding them to the generator. The manuscript references the SinSR codebase without providing an RSD implementation, and reports no seed variability or uncertainty estimates. These ambiguities matter for reproducing the objective comparisons.

Research ethics: The failure discussion is valuable, but Appendix H’s suggestion that safe training images imply low misuse risk is unjustified. Its proposed medical and autonomous-driving benefits also lack application-specific validation. These are secondary concerns; the decisive reasons for rejection are the unsupported theoretical interpretation and insufficiently controlled attribution of the empirical gains.

strengths: Significance: RSD offers a useful quality–efficiency trade-off for real-world super-resolution. Table 4 reports 174M parameters and 539 MB peak inference memory, versus 1775M and 3651 MB for OSEDiff, with comparable one-step latency.

Empirical strengths: Improvements over SinSR are substantial across several datasets. On full-size RealSR, LPIPS improves from 0.365 to 0.273 and MUSIQ from 61.582 to 65.860, while PSNR and SSIM also improve. Evaluations cover both synthetic and real degradations, and Appendix E extends the comparison to models trained at higher resolution.

Methodological merit: Proposition 3.1 provides a useful variational reformulation of denoiser matching, valid under the idealized assumption that the auxiliary model realizes the conditional mean. The distillation-only results demonstrate that improvements are not entirely attributable to supervised losses.

Presentation and reproducibility: The overall motivation and training framework are understandable. The appendices provide pseudocode, optimizer settings, update ratios, training resources, dataset sources, baseline checkpoints, and metric implementations.

Limitations and ethics: Appendix H includes concrete failure cases with ground truth and acknowledges hallucination and dependence on the teacher. This disclosure helps characterize the method’s practical boundaries.
weaknesses: Soundness—central theoretical claim: The claimed equivalence between Eq. (7) and the reverse-trajectory KL in Eq. (9)/(20) is not established. Appendix A.1, page 19, substitutes q(x_t | x̂_0, y_0) for p(x_t | y_0), asserting they are equal. A conditional forward kernel is not a marginal distribution; even after integrating over generated images, its equality to the marginal of the finite-step Gaussian reverse model in Eq. (15) is not guaranteed. An optimal conditional-mean denoiser does not generally make those Gaussian reverse transitions exact. Consequently, the joint-versus-marginal alignment interpretation and the resulting explanation of superiority over VSD lack a valid foundation.

Soundness—theoretical qualifications and errors: Proposition 3.1 implicitly assumes an exactly optimized, sufficiently expressive auxiliary model, whereas training uses five updates per generator update and additionally trains its shared features adversarially. The resulting approximation is not analyzed. Moreover, Appendices A.2–A.3 change −min of an expression into min of its negative, where max is required. The trajectory-KL derivation also needs special treatment at t=1 because the specified reverse variance vanishes. These issues matter given the prominence of the theoretical contribution.

Experimental attribution: The ResShift-VSD comparison does not isolate the distillation objective. Algorithm 2 trains its generator only from the terminal timestep, whereas RSD uses multistep training; Table 5 shows that this choice materially affects results. The full RSD model additionally receives LPIPS and GAN supervision. Matched VSD experiments with the same timestep scheme and supervised losses, together with a supervised-only control, are needed to establish the proposed objective’s incremental benefit.

Originality: Appendix A explicitly identifies close algebraic relationships to SiD/FGM and interprets RSD as a discrete version of IBMD, which already addresses image restoration. Adapting this family of objectives to latent ResShift and realistic degradations can be useful, but the manuscript overstates the novelty of the objective and does not experimentally establish the importance of retaining its particular terms relative to these closest alternatives.

Claim calibration: The broad claim of better fidelity than OSEDiff has important exceptions. On DRealSR crops in Table 3, RSD is worse in PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, MUSIQ, and MANIQA. Claims about reduced hallucination and perceptual realism rely on selected examples and proxy metrics, without a human study or systematic structural-fidelity evaluation. The evidence supports a competitive trade-off more strongly than general superiority.

Reproducibility and presentation: Algorithm 1 samples generator timesteps uniformly from all T values despite the stated N=4 configuration, and adds noise channels to the fake model while Appendix C describes adding them to the generator. Eq. (10) does not clearly specify the separate discriminator and generator objectives corresponding to the claimed standard non-saturating GAN loss. No RSD code/checkpoint link, repeated-run uncertainty, or precise loss-normalization specification is supplied.

Ethical reasoning: Appendix H’s suggestion that standard ImageNet training and the absence of unsafe training images imply low misuse risk is unsupported. The proposed medical and autonomous-driving applications also warrant acknowledgment that plausible reconstructed details can be factually wrong. This is a limitation of the impact discussion, rather than evidence of an ethical violation.
